opus-5.5.text:
I think the shift came from a growing feeling, around 2018 to 2020, that computer vision had become very good at a certain kind of problem but was missing something fundamental.

For about a decade after AlexNet, the dominant paradigm was what you might call "internet vision." You collect a huge dataset of images, people label them, and you train a model to map pixels to labels: this is a cat, this is a car, here is the bounding box, here is the segmentation mask. And we got remarkably good at that. On many benchmarks, models matched or exceeded human performance.

But if you step back, that whole setup treats vision as a passive, third-person activity. The model is a spectator. It looks at a photo someone else took, from a viewpoint someone else chose, and outputs a description. That is not how vision works in biological systems. An animal sees in order to act. It moves its head to resolve ambiguity, reaches out to touch something, pushes an object to see whether it is heavy or fixed. Perception and action form a loop.

So the conceptual shift was this: perception is not the end goal; it serves interaction with the physical world. Once you accept that, the questions you care about change. You stop asking only "what is this object?" and start asking "how do I grasp it? Where is the handle? If I pull this drawer, how will it move? What is the 3D geometry, the articulation, the physical affordance?" Those are questions a static image classifier was never designed to answer.

A few things made that shift feel urgent and feasible at the same time. First, 3D vision matured. People like me, who worked on point clouds, 6D pose estimation, and object-level 3D understanding, were already pushed toward geometry, and geometry naturally leads to manipulation, because once you know an object's shape and pose, the next thing you want to do is interact with it. Second, simulation got much better. Physics simulators and large 3D asset datasets let us put agents into environments where they could act and receive feedback, rather than only consuming fixed datasets. Third, there was a sense of diminishing returns on pure recognition benchmarks. Squeezing another half percent out of ImageNet or COCO felt less meaningful than tackling the open problem of getting a machine to actually do something useful.

Then there is a deeper argument some of us hold: real intelligence may not emerge from passive observation alone. A child learns about object permanence, gravity, and causality partly by interacting, dropping things, stacking blocks, making mistakes. If you want machines to have that grounded understanding of the physical world, they probably need a body, or at least a simulated one, and they need to learn through the consequences of their own actions.

So embodied AI, for vision researchers, was a reorientation: from "seeing to describe" to "seeing to act." And honestly, once you make that turn, it is very hard to go back. The problems become much harder, because data is scarce, the real world is messy, and sim-to-real gaps are painful. But they also become much more meaningful, because they connect directly to robots that can eventually work in homes, factories, and everyday life.

r001.rationale: The response contrasts passive viewing of fixed images with active observation, including moving one’s head to resolve ambiguity, and describes perception and action as a loop.

r002.rationale: The response says vision serves interaction with the physical world and gives examples of reaching, pushing, and learning from the consequences of actions.

fable-5.1.text:
I think the core shift was realizing that perception, by itself, had hit a ceiling in what it could tell us about intelligence.

For a long time, computer vision was essentially a passive discipline. You collect a dataset of images or videos from the internet, you label them, you train a model to recognize or detect or segment things, and then you measure accuracy on a held-out set. And that paradigm was incredibly productive. ImageNet, deep learning, the whole revolution of the 2010s came out of it. But around 2017 or 2018, a lot of us started noticing that the models were getting very good at answering "what is in this picture" while being essentially useless at answering "what should I do next."

And that gap is not a small engineering gap. It's conceptual. In the passive paradigm, the model is an observer. The data distribution is fixed, it's decided by whoever scraped the web. The model never chooses where to look, never gets to test a hypothesis, never experiences the consequences of being wrong. Biological vision didn't evolve that way at all. Vision evolved in service of action. An animal sees in order to move, to grasp, to avoid things. Perception and action are a loop, not a pipeline.

So the shift was moving from "vision as recognition" to "vision as something an agent does inside an environment." Once you accept that framing, several things change at once. The agent generates its own data by interacting. The evaluation metric is no longer label accuracy but task success. And things that were previously ignored by vision people, like physics, like 3D geometry, like contact and manipulation, suddenly become central, because you cannot act in the world without modeling how the world responds to you.

I'd add that simulation played a big role in making this feel practical rather than just philosophical. Once we had environments like AI2-THOR, Habitat, SAPIEN, where you could drop an agent in and let it move around and interact at scale, researchers from a vision background could actually run experiments in this loop without first becoming roboticists. That lowered the barrier enormously.

For me personally, the thing that really convinced me was working on articulated objects and grasping. You can label a cabinet in an image all day, but understanding a cabinet means knowing where the handle is, which way the drawer slides, how much force it takes. That knowledge only reveals itself when you try to open it. That's when I felt the field had to move toward embodiment, not as a new application of vision but as a different definition of what seeing is for.

r001.rationale: The response contrasts fixed, passively collected data with an agent that chooses where to look and generates data through interaction.

r002.rationale: It describes perception as a loop with action and says agents interact with the environment and experience the consequences of their actions.

astra-6.text:
I think the key shift was from asking, “How can a machine recognize what’s in an image?” to asking, “How can an intelligent agent use what it sees to act in the world?” In traditional computer vision, we often give a model a fixed image or video and ask it to predict a label, detect an object, or estimate geometry. But for an embodied agent, perception is part of a loop: it observes, acts, changes its relationship to the environment, and observes again.

Imagine a robot trying to pick up a cup. Recognizing the cup is only the beginning. It needs to understand where it can grasp it, how to reach it, and whether it should move to get a better view. Its task determines what it needs to perceive, and its actions can help resolve uncertainty.

So the conceptual shift is toward studying perception, action, and learning together. Vision becomes a capability that supports interaction with the world, and interaction becomes a way to develop better understanding.

r001.rationale: It contrasts fixed images with an agent that acts and observes again, including moving to get a better view.

r002.rationale: It says actions change the agent’s relationship to the environment and describes the robot reaching for or moving around the cup.

sol-6.1.text:
I think the key shift was from seeing intelligence as passive observation to seeing it as active interaction. In traditional computer vision, we give a model an image or a video and ask it to recognize what is there. But an embodied agent has to decide what to do: where to look, where to move, what to touch, and how to change its surroundings to achieve a goal.

That creates a loop between perception and action. If an object is partly hidden, the agent can move to get a better view. If it wants to understand how an object behaves, it can interact with it. So perception is no longer an isolated task; it supports action, and action produces new information. That is the conceptual move toward embodied AI: understanding intelligence through an agent’s interaction with the world.

r001.rationale: It contrasts passive image or video recognition with an agent actively deciding where to look and move, making active observation part of the shift.

r002.rationale: It says the agent can touch objects and change its surroundings to achieve a goal, identifying environmental influence as part of the shift.
